operator_plays.name: GSA & Municipal Set-Aside Pass-Through Facility Ghost-Brokering
operator_plays.mechanism: Match eligible facility-service primes with disclosed qualified subcontractors and earn documented coordination fees; opaque pass-throughs and false set-aside eligibility are excluded.
inputs: Licensed local vendor bids and capacity records
workflow: 1. Screen solicitations for service scope, eligibility, and permitted subcontracting
2. Verify the prime performs required work and disclose broker and subcontractor roles
3. Submit priced delivery plans with genuine vendor commitments and required certifications
4. Track service acceptance, payroll obligations, and authorized fee payments against contract terms

platform_risks.failure_mode: Set-aside eligibility protest or prohibited pass-through finding
platform_risks.trigger: Inaccurate certification or subcontracting beyond contract limits
platform_risks.impact: Termination, repayment demands, or debarment exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unverified certifications and subcontracted work share versus permitted limits
platform_risks.fallback: Withdraw noncompliant bids and operate as a disclosed subcontractor on unrestricted work

operator_plays.name: Commercial Hail-Swath Public Adjuster & Appraisal-Clause Storm Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Match verified commercial storm damage with licensed public-adjuster capacity and policy-specific appraisal processes, distinguishing valuation disputes from coverage questions.
inputs: Public hail-swath data and property records
Policy forms and dated damage inspections
State licensing, solicitation, and fee-limit rules
workflow: 1. Map storm footprints to commercial properties and conduct permitted owner outreach
2. Obtain authorized inspections and licensed review of coverage, deadlines, and preexisting damage
3. Submit supported estimates and invoke appraisal only where the policy and dispute allow it
4. Reconcile settlement, repairs, and lawful disclosed fees without inflating losses
metrics: Days from inspection to resolved valuation
Net client proceeds after fees and deductible

platform_risks.failure_mode: Unauthorized adjusting or inapplicable appraisal demand
platform_risks.trigger: Unlicensed solicitation or use of appraisal to resolve excluded coverage issues
platform_risks.impact: Claim delay, fee forfeiture, and licensing penalties
platform_risks.detection_metric: License exceptions and appraisal requests rejected for coverage disputes
platform_risks.fallback: Pause solicitation and refer coverage disputes to qualified counsel while licensed adjusters handle supported valuations

operator_plays.name: MCA UCC-1 Trigger Stacking & Dual-Sided Default-Restructure Brokerage
operator_plays.mechanism: Use UCC filing changes to identify businesses that may need cash-flow review and consensual MCA restructuring, with verified obligations and disclosed compensation rather than encouraging undisclosed stacking.
inputs: Public UCC filings and termination records
Broker licensing rules and disclosed creditor compensation terms
workflow: 1. Treat UCC changes as outreach signals, not proof of default, and obtain merchant authorization
2. Reconcile advances, liens, repayment pulls, covenants, and sustainable payment capacity
3. Disclose dual-sided fees and conflicts; use independent counsel where representation would conflict
4. Coordinate documented creditor-approved modifications and monitor actual payment relief
metrics: Net merchant payment relief after fees

platform_risks.failure_mode: Conflicted brokerage or prohibited stacking worsens default
platform_risks.trigger: Hidden commissions, inaccurate balances, or new financing breaching existing contracts
platform_risks.detection_metric: Undisclosed fee exceptions and covenant breaches per engagement
platform_risks.fallback: Stop placement, refund improper fees, and refer the merchant to independent licensed restructuring counsel

operator_plays.name: TCPA Serial-Plaintiff Docket Scraping & Real-Time Litigator-Scrub Firewall Tollbooth
operator_plays.mechanism: Offer consent-first outbound compliance screening using lawful docket-derived risk signals alongside mandatory do-not-call and revocation checks; plaintiff matching neither authorizes contact nor replaces TCPA compliance.
inputs: Permitted public docket data with identity confidence scores
Consent provenance, revocations, and suppression lists
Applicable calling rules and customer retention policies
workflow: 1. Ingest permitted docket records with source dates, minimization, and human identity review
2. Check consent, do-not-call status, revocations, and calling restrictions before optional risk enrichment
3. Suppress noncompliant contacts and route uncertain matches to review without planting honeypots or provoking claims
4. Serve auditable screening decisions with correction, deletion, and retention controls
metrics: Contacts blocked for missing consent or suppression match

platform_risks.failure_mode: False identity match or false assurance of permission to call
platform_risks.trigger: Stale docket data or treating absence from a plaintiff list as consent
platform_risks.impact: Unlawful outreach, privacy complaints, and customer liability
platform_risks.detection_metric: Consent-audit failure rate and upheld identity correction requests
platform_risks.fallback: Disable uncertain enrichment and require independently verified consent and authoritative suppression checks

chapters.question_prompt: How do practitioners actually start a cleaning business from little or no money, and what did the founders who scaled to six and seven figures do differently?
chapters.title: Starting Lean: Founder Playbooks from Zero to Seven Figures
chapters.subtitle: Launching under $1,000 or with no money, solo operation, essential supplies and equipment, top-to-bottom commercial cleaning training, UK business plans, and founder case studies from million-dollar cleaning, Queen Bee, and pool-cleaning operators
chapters.executive_summary: Founders building from zero toward seven figures agree on a lean sequence: learn the work hands-on, price for the labor you will eventually hire, and win recurring contracts through reputation and fast follow-up. AJ Simmons runs a sub-$1,000 launch built on a $99 CBN membership, a $200 LLC budget, a $25 domain and 400 cold calls in week one, deferring insurance and supplies until a deal closes. DJ The Boss landed a first lead for $1.75 in Google Ads that grew into roughly $500K over seven years, then burned $6K on the same campaign. UpFlip's operator runs 60% labor and nets 15-20%. Practitioners split on whether owners must clean first or whether inexperience is an advantage, and on paperwork: Nicole Thomas holds seven commercial buildings without an LLC, EIN, insurance or website.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Scaled operators keep returning to one premise: you must understand the work before you can sell or manage it. The $15M owner interviewed by AJ Simmons tells first-year founders to do everything themselves first, mastering chemicals, equipment, supplies, training and hiring, and warns that owners who have never cleaned are not going to make it far [7pVd69Als0I @ 00:00:57]. That company forces every six-figure management hire, including the CTO of its software arm, to clean for 30 days so they learn changed locks, forgotten keys and locked supply closets in the field. AJ backs that up from their own franchise start at 19, when no training meant smeared windows and skipped tasks on a children's clinic worth about $2K+ per month [srB5UatlJlU @ 00:07:49]. Clean Ops Guide frames the same lesson from the buyer side: commercial cleaning is a professional service business, not just cleaning buildings, and property managers are paying for reliability, communication and peace of mind so they never have to chase the crew [IgZO8_dFaeU @ 00:00:16]. The shared baseline is simple: know the labor, know the site problems, and sell certainty rather than mop strokes to every buyer.

The second point of agreement is that the real asset is the recurring contract, not the one-off job. Clean Ops Guide lays out the commercial cadence, an office three evenings a week, a medical facility five nights, a large building daily, and notes that a single client can mean hundreds of visits over several years [IgZO8_dFaeU @ 00:02:35]. DJ The Boss proves the compounding: a gymnastics facility signed on a 12-month agreement grew from two days to five days a week, and when the point of contact moved to another facility, the contact brought the company along, turning client one into contract two [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:00:53]. AJ Simmons tells owners to optimize for keeping a contract five years rather than squeezing profit from it today, backed by a policy that a no-call/no-show is an automatic firing [srB5UatlJlU @ 00:21:19]. The threat to that asset is rarely cleaning quality. AJ warns that a competitor met at a Chamber of Commerce event can take an account on relationship alone, so solo operators still run daytime inspections at least quarterly and keep communication constant [mp0PpDrOpYM @ 00:04:57]. Retention, in this playbook, is a sales activity that never stops after the signature.

Speed and public reputation close the loop. Ricky Regalado, running a roughly $10M Chicago operation, says walkthroughs die when proposals are not turned around quickly, so the proposal goes out within two to three hours of the walkthrough [QBuGc_Q36dg @ 00:05:39]. AJ Simmons pushes the same discipline downstream: call within 24 hours, tell the prospect to check spam, follow up again after about a week, and keep going until there is a clear yes or no, because deals have closed six months later and many owners lose business simply by not following up [pqTeTRcPhKg @ 00:20:13]. Reputation is the other half. Joel Davis says Google reviews are what sells the business, with the web page plus Google PPC and reviews producing the best return on their pool route [j3l2-xKJKb8 @ 00:29:01]. UpFlip's $120K-per-month residential operator calls clients the next day for feedback and responds to every review, crediting the protected online reputation as one of the keys to fast growth [d4Iip7BHXwg @ 00:18:25]. Across commercial, residential and pool service, the consensus is identical: answer fast, follow up until the prospect decides, and treat star ratings as the storefront prospects actually check before calling.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: AJ Simmons lays out a launch target of under $1,000 and a first customer inside 30 days. Step one is the $99 CBN membership through a special link to dodge the setup fee, canceled if no customer lands in 30 days; bookkeeping runs on free waveapps.com; the LLC typically costs $100 to $125 with $200 budgeted, while the EIN and BOI filing are free; five bid appointments cost $625 at $125 each; the domain runs $25 max and a Canva print order about $50 [VrlDbQP4iQI @ 00:05:27]. AJ's 2026 course adds the insurance spec to quote but not yet buy: $1M per incident and $2M aggregate, with the line that the business should pay for itself [pqTeTRcPhKg @ 00:06:01]. The residential benchmark from UpFlip ran higher at $5K: $4K for a 2003 Accord, a $500 vacuum, $300 in supplies and the rest on flyers, or about $1K for anyone who already owns a car [d4Iip7BHXwg @ 00:03:07]. Kadz Money started UK domestic work with a Home Bargains box of about £20, sponges and five or six cloths, carrying no vacuum or mop because the insurance did not cover a vacuum [dEkotRT-f90 @ 00:01:36]. Capital is not the bottleneck in any of these builds.

The acquisition math is explicit. AJ's calling plan is 100 businesses Monday through Friday: 400 calls in week one should yield one to four walkthroughs, and 1,500 more over the remaining weeks should produce four to 20 appointments, one to four contracts and about $2K per month recurring [VrlDbQP4iQI @ 00:14:20]. DJ The Boss went paid instead: after wasting $600 on door hangers, they built a website because competitors had no online presence, ran Google's free $100 ad credit on a badly configured campaign drawing clicks from the Philippines and China, and still caught the first lead at $1.75 of spend [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:06:17]. UpFlip's operator budgets roughly $4K a month on Google Local Leads, which bills per call and allows disputed leads, plus $1K on Facebook and $700 to $750 on Yelp, with Google performing best; in slow December-to-February months they text a $50-off offer to 1,500 contacts through HighLevel and see at least 10% reply [d4Iip7BHXwg @ 00:04:21]. Kadz Money's cheap UK channels mirror this: a Gumtree ad at £5 to £10 a month pulled about 28 inquiries, and a £10 Mumsnet ad still generates calls years later [dEkotRT-f90 @ 00:03:01].

Pricing starts at the walkthrough, and the practitioners script it tightly. Ricky Regalado arrives on time, shakes hands, asks about the client's hot points, never requests a scope of work, prices the facility and the person's expectations, and closes with a same-type reference, restaurant to restaurant or luxury high-rise to luxury high-rise [QBuGc_Q36dg @ 00:04:54]. AJ Simmons wears a logo shirt, brings a second person to measure and record, asks about pain points, budget and frequency, never promises a delivery time, never prices on the spot, and runs the numbers through calculatedclean.app afterward [pqTeTRcPhKg @ 00:17:46]. Measurement drives the bid: AJ's supply list puts a laser measure on the cleanable square footage only, because a 10,000-foot building where you clean 2,000 feet will get bid way too high [mk-8avM72Ms @ 00:02:52]. DJ The Boss adds the margin rule that built a $500K account: ask the client's budget, price it to include the employees you will eventually put in, come in under the incumbent ServiceMaster after its roughly 35% hike, bill in advance and collect upfront; that client now pays about triple the original rate [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:09:39]. Price for future labor, not for your own free hours.

callout.title: Cash-Light Moves the Operators Actually Run
callout.body: These are the street-level shortcuts practitioners use to close before spending and to reopen dead deals.
items: Buy no cleaning supplies until a deal closes; push for upfront payment, otherwise net 10 or net 15, and if cash is short, borrow or sub the job out while working alongside the subcontractor [AJ SIMMONS — VrlDbQP4iQI @ 00:16:03]
Get insurance quoted but hold the purchase: AJ advises answering 'yes' when asked about insurance and buying the policy only when a deal is ready to close [AJ SIMMONS — VrlDbQP4iQI @ 00:15:12]
When a lost bid resurfaces, resend the same proposal with a couple percent added for inflation; Ricky Regalado had the contract signed in two hours [AJ SIMMONS — QBuGc_Q36dg @ 00:08:07]
Pull up on construction trailers at 5 to 6 AM to catch project managers and general contractors in person, the way Charles Banks fed post-construction work [AJ SIMMONS — du4OAGZv9AE @ 00:15:26]

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the founder playbook is how much legal scaffolding goes up before the first invoice. AJ Simmons tells even solo operators to still form an LLC, both to shield personal assets when someone slips on a wet floor with no sign posted and because businesses prefer paying licensed and insured vendors [mp0PpDrOpYM @ 00:01:28]. The 2026 course runs the full stack: articles of organization for a single-member LLC, a free EIN, a business bank account for deductions, and a business license or sales-tax registration only where required [pqTeTRcPhKg @ 00:03:33]. Nicole Thomas in Lake Charles runs the opposite experiment and reports seven commercial buildings with nobody asking for an LLC, an EIN, insurance, or a website, while still admitting "I know I need to do that" [NHWdv_WG2B8 @ 00:05:46]. Insurance timing splits even inside the AJ camp: the under-$1,000 plan says answer yes when a prospect asks about coverage but only buy the policy once a deal is ready to close, and buy no supplies until then either [VrlDbQP4iQI @ 00:15:12]. The working read for an operator: the lean camp defers spending, not structure, and every speaker who skipped paperwork still treats it as a debt to settle once contracts land. Thomas covers the gap with client references instead of a website and has clients order Thomas's preferred supplies.

Whether the founder needs to have pushed a mop is the second live disagreement. The $15 million cleaning company owner interviewed by AJ Simmons says new owners have to do everything themselves first, covering cleaning, chemicals, equipment, supplies, training and hiring, and that owners who have never cleaned are not going to make it that far [7pVd69Als0I @ 00:00:57]. That owner sends every six-figure management hire, including the CTO of the software company, into the field for 30 days to learn changed locks, forgotten keys, locked supply closets and alarm issues [7pVd69Als0I @ 00:01:29]. Jazmine Tates flips the premise: never having cleaned professionally might be the advantage, because experienced cleaners think like a cleaner and not like a CEO, and cleaning skills can be outsourced while systems cannot [g8OVdfYHogY @ 00:01:19]. AJ lands between the two, having cleaned roughly nine years personally yet telling founders to hire people from day one and to drive Uber or take a job rather than live off the company too early [srB5UatlJlU @ 00:16:38]. Tates's own hiring filter demands contractors with at least two years of residential experience, their own supplies and reliable transport, so field knowledge still enters the business. It just does not have to live in the owner, whose job becomes coordination rather than supervision.

Customer acquisition splits into an outbound grind and an inbound reputation play. AJ Simmons scripts the grind: 100 business calls Monday through Friday, roughly 400 in week one for one to four walkthroughs, then 1,500 more for four to twenty appointments, one to four contracts and about $2,000 a month recurring [VrlDbQP4iQI @ 00:14:20]. Ricky Regalado, running about a $10 million Chicago operation, says the company does no marketing, cold calling or email campaigns, names Google reviews as the number one source, and says every new caller mentions the reviews [QBuGc_Q36dg @ 00:03:06]. Paid search sits in the middle and cuts both ways: DJ The Boss landed the gymnastics facility off a lead that cost $1.75 in ad spend, then burned $6,000 on the same campaign with no other business to speak of [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:08:47]. The UpFlip residential operator spends about $4,000 a month on Google Local Leads, pays per call, disputes junk leads, and ranks Google above Facebook at $1,000 and Yelp at $700 to $750 [d4Iip7BHXwg @ 00:04:21]. DJ's verdict reconciles the camps: Google Ads is the answer but not the answer, because you still have to be good at Google Ads, and cost per click drops when your SEO is at least somewhat set up.

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common first-year loss is money spent on the wrong channel or a price set before the operator knows the job. DJ The Boss opened with $600 of door hangers and calls it a dumb move, because hangers suit residential and the target was commercial; flyers in mailboxes did produce the first post-construction jobs [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:04:14]. The Google Ads campaign that followed ran with negative-keyword problems and the wrong geo-targeting, pulling clicks from the Philippines and China before the $1.75 lead arrived [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:05:59]. Underpricing hits just as hard. The UpFlip operator's first move-out paid $90 for about 12 hours of work, and the fix was calling competitors for a three-bed, two-bath quote before pricing again [d4Iip7BHXwg @ 00:17:26]. Kadz Money started at £10 to £12 an hour in the UK, now recommends £15 to £20 with the first clean at half price, and pushes per-job or annual pricing such as £600 a year [dEkotRT-f90 @ 00:05:57]. Kadz also flags clients who try to squeeze a three-to-six-hour clean into two hours, countered with a free walkthrough using a room-by-room clipboard and a direct question about what the last cleaner failed at, which is usually reliability.

Cash conversion is where lean founders get squeezed. Charles Banks hit $30,000 a month inside a franchise yet kept roughly half after deductions and fees, with a crew still to pay out of that half [du4OAGZv9AE @ 00:06:12]. Banks also reports jobs that went unpaid and says they are still waiting on the money [du4OAGZv9AE @ 00:10:53]. AJ Simmons puts the timing bluntly: commercial franchise work pays effectively net 60, so everything you do this month arrives at the end of next month, while residential pays faster with better margins [srB5UatlJlU @ 00:32:58]. Clean Ops Guide warns that a 50,000 square foot building demands multiple employees, more equipment, supervision, and enough cash to cover payroll before the invoice is paid, and tells new owners to start under 5,000 square feet [IgZO8_dFaeU @ 00:03:14]. The counter-moves practitioners actually used: DJ The Boss billed in advance and got paid upfront after pricing under a ServiceMaster that had raised rates about 35 percent, and AJ asks for upfront payment or net 10 to net 15. AJ's own exit from field cleaning came with debt and repossessed cars, offset only by having a system that finally ran without AJ in it.

The failure that does not show up on a profit sheet is people. DJ The Boss, roughly seven years and about $500,000 into a single contract, says sales is easy and managing people is the hard part [ZVDOV6jG8Dw @ 00:10:51]. AJ Simmons warns solo operators that even great cleaning loses to a relationship: a competitor met at a Chamber of Commerce event can take the account, so daytime inspections at least quarterly and steady communication are the defense [mp0PpDrOpYM @ 00:04:57]. Ricky Regalado names the sales-side version, walkthroughs wasted because the proposal did not go out quickly, and sets a two-to-three-hour turnaround; Regalado also admits showing up late ruined one walkthrough [QBuGc_Q36dg @ 00:05:39]. Nicole Thomas hit the reverse problem: clients got too attached to Thomas personally, which blocks handing off accounts, so Thomas's daughter now comes along from the first visit [NHWdv_WG2B8 @ 00:18:21]. AJ's no-call/no-show rule is automatic firing, and a nine-hour relocation forced backup plans B, C and D plus invoice credits to keep contracts alive. The goal AJ sets is keeping a contract five years rather than squeezing profit from it today.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I turn a first walkthrough into a signed commercial cleaning contract and onboard the new client correctly?
chapters.title: Landing the First Contract: Walkthrough, Proposal, Close, Onboard
chapters.subtitle: Live coaching calls from zero, residential-to-commercial transitions, walkthrough tactics, qualifying-position closing, differentiated proposals and contract write-ups, winning without being the cheapest, and new-client onboarding checklists
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on a blunt reality: roughly 90% of commercial prospects already have a cleaner, so the first contract is won on dependability, pain diagnosis and follow-through rather than the lowest bid. AJ Simmons runs a phone-first machine of 100 calls a day, projecting 10-20 appointments and 1-2 closes a month, while Mike Mak and Commercial Cleaning CEO lean on power-base referrals, BNI and free proof cleans. Pricing runs on production rates, not square footage: Joseph D Adams uses 3,500-4,000 sq ft per hour for offices and targets a 30% margin. OctoClean Media pushes a pain-decision-budget qualification and floats a number 25-30% higher when budgets stall. The splits: AJ's relentless 'wearsome' follow-up versus Clean Ops Guide's respect for the client's timeline, and whether a website and Google profile matter at all.

key_metrics.label: Cold-Call Funnel Output
key_metrics.value: 100 calls/day = 2,000/month -> 10-20 appointments -> at least 1-2 closes
key_metrics.context: AJ Simmons projects each month of calling adds $1,000-2,000 in recurring revenue, reaching $10-12k/month and six figures within one year.

key_metrics.value: 3,500-4,000 sq ft per hour
key_metrics.context: Joseph D Adams of Green Line Operations converts footage into labor hours, with a worked example of 6,000 divided by 25 equaling 2.4 hours.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The first contract is a trust sale before it is a cleaning sale. Joseph Adams of Clean Ops Guide frames the buyer's core question as whether you are 'dependable,' because a cleaning crew gets unsupervised, after-hours access to the building [XySWgKh0nEY @ 00:00:17]. Janitorial Empire says the same thing in commercial terms: clients buy reliability, and the starting kit is a professional email, phone number, capability information and insurance documentation, aimed first at small offices before medical, dental, daycare, churches, retail and small warehouses, with the first account doing double duty as the reference that sells the next one [8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:00:29]. AJ Simmons adds the hard market fact that shapes every pitch: '90%' of prospects already have a cleaner, and a prospect with no cleaner usually has no budget, so that prospect gets skipped [Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:03:35]. AJ also narrows the target map. Skyscrapers, anything that says 'go through corporate' or 'vendors list,' and connected buildings run by a management company that may only issue RFPs 'once a year' are out; individually managed standalone or medium-size buildings are in [ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:02:58]. The operator takeaway is consistent across these voices: start small, start reachable, and walk in assuming you are displacing an incumbent whose weak spot is reliability and service, not price.

Price is not the battlefield these practitioners choose. OctoClean Media's 30-year sales veteran qualifies every deal on three axes, pain, decision and budget, and opens by asking 'why am I here'; if the answer is the lowest possible bid, the account is not a fit and the seller walks [1tf8JMWxi98 @ 00:01:04]. Cleaning Launch, whose host reports building a $5M+ company, states flatly that clients do not pick the cheapest quote and that lowballers should be ignored [V84a_KWRYU4 @ 00:00:15]. OctoClean Media's proposal video goes further, noting that some winners are the highest bidder and that proposals lose by being interchangeable rather than expensive [OzSRs5osKKI @ 00:00:32]. AJ Simmons reports the switching order from the field: service first, then price, then communication and relationship, and AJ digs it out with one question, 'How are you guys handling your cleaning services right now?' [Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:04:39]. The answers to AJ's question decode the incumbent's weakness: 'We got a lady' signals under-the-table help, and in-house cleaning signals dust, which is why high dusting sits in AJ's routine. The shared rule is to diagnose the incumbent's failure in the buyer's own words and price against that failure, not against the cheapest competitor in the local market.

The walkthrough is where practitioners agree the contract is actually won or lost. Janitorial Empire's checklist covers square footage, restrooms, offices, flooring, headcount, frequency, kitchens, consumables, security and complaints about the current cleaner, and the channel's verdict on bidding is blunt: 'Winning a contract that loses money isn't winning' [8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:04:28]. Joseph D Adams of Green Line Operations, with 25 years in the trade and a full-time job still running, admits on the ONLY MAIDS PODCAST hot seat that the very first job was underbid [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:05:40]. Clean Ops Guide warns that two 10,000 sq ft offices can carry completely different workloads, so flooring, restrooms and high-touch areas get inspected and the client gets heard instead of the footage simply being plugged into a formula [XySWgKh0nEY @ 00:02:50]. Follow-up closes the consensus loop. Janitorial Empire observes that 'a surprising amount of business is won simply because one company followed up while another didn't,' and pairs it with a simple rule: send scope, frequency, monthly price and terms, then follow up after a few business days [8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:04:59]. Across all three channels the pattern holds: measure honestly, price for profit, and be the company still in contact when the incumbent slips.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: AJ Simmons runs the most explicit numbers game: 100 calls a day, 500 a week, 2,000 a month, which AJ projects into 10 to 20 appointments and at least one to two closes, each adding $1,000 to $2,000 a month until the book reaches $10,000 to $12,000 monthly and six figures inside a year [ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:03:56]. The opener asks for 'the person in charge of hiring the cleaning company,' and appointments are always proposed two to three days out at 10:00. Joseph D Adams works a slower, part-time cadence while holding a full-time job: five businesses a week, roughly 20 a month, leaving a business card and capability statement to land two or three walkthroughs a month [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:01:00]. Janitorial Empire builds the list from Google Maps, logging name, address, phone, website, contact and date, and argues that '50 qualified prospects' beat hundreds of random calls [8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:02:03]. Mike Mak, ten years in, found cold calling, door-to-door, Bark and Yelp produced cheapest-bid clients and pivoted to warm channels: the doctor, car dealership or chiropractor already in your life, plus BNI groups of 15 to 30 people that Mak expects to yield three to four offices [G2qoM4LqGdM @ 00:04:46].

Pricing mechanics center on production rates rather than square-foot guesses. OctoClean Media calls bidding by the square foot a 'rookie mistake' and has estimators go room by room, counting sinks and toilets and photographing dispensers and hot spots before any number is built [j_wLBMK7Flk @ 00:02:25]. Joseph D Adams supplies the actual rates: 3,500 to 4,000 sq ft per hour for offices, medical spoken as '22 to 28,' and a worked example of 6,000 sq ft divided by 25 landing at 2.4 hours [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:05:57]. On margin, Adams targets 30 percent: a $2,100 cost becomes a $3,000 price and $900 profit, going as low as about 25 percent for strategic accounts [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:07:34]. Janitorial Empire lists the cost stack that has to sit under that price, labor hours, payroll burden, supplies, equipment, transport, insurance, overhead and profit, and shows the hour math with three hours a night across five nights coming to about 65 hours a month [8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:04:28]. The same channel warns that underbidding damages the company. The street sequence is therefore fixed: count fixtures, convert footage into hours with a production rate, load the full cost stack, then add margin before the proposal is written, and refuse to bid below it.

The close runs on qualification scripts and speed. OctoClean Media never asks 'what's your budget'; the question is what solving the problem is 'worth,' and when a buyer resists, the line is 'we're going to be too high, should we stop now,' followed by a number floated 25 to 30 percent higher [1tf8JMWxi98 @ 00:04:18]. Joseph D Adams sends the proposal within 24 hours of the walkthrough, so the numbers land while the visit is still fresh in the buyer's mind [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:09:17]. AJ Simmons compresses it further into a 'wearsome' cadence: walkthrough in the morning, proposal by the afternoon, a call before the contact gets off work, never more than a week between touches, and no stopping until the prospect says stop [Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:07:43]. Cleaning Launch adds a framing move: present a top-to-bottom deep clean, normally 'a premium charge,' as included because the contract is recurring, knowing the first clean takes about double the time anyway [V84a_KWRYU4 @ 00:04:16]. Decision mapping matters too; OctoClean Media calls 'are you the decision maker' a rookie move and asks instead how the last decision was made, by committee or by one person. Each tactic shortens the gap between interest and signature while keeping price anchored to value rather than to the cheapest bid.

callout.title: Walkthrough and Close Moves From the Field
callout.body: Small, repeatable moves the practitioners use to read the building, handle the incumbent objection and make the proposal travel up the chain [AJ SIMMONS — IMsJ1NxKfUk @ 00:02:41].
items: Arrive 20 minutes early and use the lobby wait to scan for cobwebs, ledge dust, floor smudges and window fingerprints, and start measuring with a laser measure [AJ SIMMONS — IMsJ1NxKfUk @ 00:04:13].
When the point of contact tests you, check partition ledges, window ledges, blinds and toilet bolts, but judge when to show it off and when not to [AJ SIMMONS — Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:05:39].
When the prospect already has a cleaner, offer a complimentary quote to keep 'on file' in case the current vendor 'drops the ball' [AJ SIMMONS — ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:05:20].
Make the proposal forwardable: you are likely talking to an influencer, so the document has to stand on its own when passed up the chain [OctoClean Media — j_wLBMK7Flk @ 00:03:41].

sop_steps.title: Build and Work a Qualified List
sop_steps.action: Pull qualified prospects from Google Maps and call for the person who hires the cleaning company.
sop_steps.detail: Log name, address, phone, website, contact and date for 50 qualified prospects rather than hundreds of random calls [Janitorial Empire — 8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:01:48], then ask for 'the person in charge of hiring the cleaning company' and book the walkthrough [AJ SIMMONS — ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:00:29].

sop_steps.title: Run the Walkthrough Like an Inventory
sop_steps.action: Go room by room, count fixtures, photograph hot spots and ask the pain question.
sop_steps.detail: Count sinks and toilets and photograph dispensers and hot spots [OctoClean Media — j_wLBMK7Flk @ 00:01:56], and ask 'How are you guys handling your cleaning services right now?' to surface the incumbent's failure [AJ SIMMONS — Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:04:39].

sop_steps.title: Price From Production Rates and Margin
sop_steps.action: Convert footage to labor hours, load full cost, then add a 30 percent margin.

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is how the first contract gets sourced. AJ Simmons runs a pure phone machine: 100 calls a day, 500 a week, 2,000 a month, feeding 10 to 20 appointments and at least 1 to 2 closes, with each month stacking $1,000 to $2,000 until the book reaches $10,000 to $12,000 a month. He says social posts, ads, a Google My Business profile and a fancy website are not needed [ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:04:27], and he ranks the phone over door-to-door because it is quicker and burns no gas [ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:09:53]. Mike Mak, ten years in, reports the opposite result from cold outreach: cold calling, door-to-door, Bark and Yelp delivered clients who only wanted the cheapest bid [G2qoM4LqGdM @ 00:01:12]. His replacement is the power base, meaning the doctor, the car dealership or the chiropractor seen every two weeks, plus a BNI chapter of 15 to 30 people where he expects 3 to 4 offices. Matt of Commercial Cleaning CEO leans toward Mak, insisting the business is relationship-based even when leads arrive through Google Ads or cold email, and he pushes beginners to work referrals and introductions first [SU1OB2thaKo @ 00:05:04]. The operator choice is volume dialing versus warm network leverage, and the two camps report very different lead quality.

Follow-up intensity is the second fault line. AJ Simmons preaches being 'wearsome': walkthrough in the morning, proposal by the afternoon, a phone call before the prospect gets off work, and never stopping until they tell you to, with no more than one week between contacts [Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:07:43]. Joseph Adams of Clean Ops Guide runs a softer cadence: confirm receipt, offer clarification, track every communication and 'respect the client's timeline,' while warning, 'Don't assume you lost the contract' [XySWgKh0nEY @ 00:05:07]. Both agree silence kills deals; they disagree on how hard to lean. The two camps also report different odds. AJ tells operators nobody closes 100 percent and that a single lead is '50/50' [Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:11:53]. The Cleaning Launch host, who reports building a $5M-plus company, frames a typical closing rate of 10 percent and claims anti-cheap positioning lifts it to 25 to 35 percent [V84a_KWRYU4 @ 00:01:22]. That positioning tells the prospect outright, 'We won't be the cheapest,' then backs it with good wages, frequent inspections, same-day response and fixing problems at the company's own cost. Run AJ's math and one appointment is a coin flip; run the Cleaning Launch math and you need roughly three to four proposals per win, so budget prospecting volume accordingly.

Qualifying and pricing method split along the same line. OctoClean Media's 30-year salesman calls 'what's your budget' the wrong question: ask what solving the problem is worth, and if the prospect stonewalls, say 'we're going to be too high, should we stop now' and float a number 25 to 30 percent higher [1tf8JMWxi98 @ 00:04:18]. AJ Simmons goes direct, asking about budget or what the account currently pays during the walkthrough itself [Xvc-7yo1lng @ 00:11:19]. On the bid math, AJ's door-to-door method grabs the square footage and runs it through the Clean Business Network bidding calculator [ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:01:01]. OctoClean labels bidding by the square foot a rookie mistake and builds price from production rates after a room-by-room inventory that counts sinks and toilets and photographs dispensers and hot spots [j_wLBMK7Flk @ 00:02:25]. The practical difference: the calculator camp can quote from a door knock and a number, while the production-rate camp needs a full walkthrough before any price leaves the building. OctoClean adds that if the prospect's stated reason for the meeting is the lowest possible bid, you are not a fit and should walk. AJ instead keeps low-intent prospects warm with a complimentary quote kept on file in case the incumbent drops the ball.

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Underbidding is the failure practitioners own up to most directly. Joseph D Adams of Green Line Operations, with 25 years in the trade, says his first job was underbid [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:05:40]. His fix is production-rate and margin discipline: offices run at 3,500 to 4,000 square feet an hour, and his worked example divides 6,000 square feet by 25 to land at 2.4 hours. Then comes a 30 percent margin target: $2,100 in cost priced at $3,000 leaves $900 in profit, and he has dropped to about 25 percent only for strategic accounts [aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:07:34]. Janitorial Empire prices from labor hours, payroll burden, supplies, equipment, transport, insurance, overhead and profit, using a 3-hour, 5-night account at roughly 65 hours a month, and warns flatly that underbidding damages the company [8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:04:42]. Clean Ops Guide attacks the same trap from capacity: a small office can beat a medical facility, so check facility needs, staff capacity and profitability, because winning work you cannot manage 'isn't growth' [XySWgKh0nEY @ 00:02:33]. The economics check is simple: if labor hours times your loaded cost leave less than the margin floor, the contract is a loss you are paying to keep, and every extra night of it compounds the damage.

The second cluster of losses happens before price is even weighed. The Cleaning Launch host reports losing a $50,000-a-year contract, a quarter million dollars over five years, because the proposal never mentioned security practices: the alarm, the locks, the lights and calling security. Despite the most competitive quote, they finished 'second best' [V84a_KWRYU4 @ 00:07:28]. AJ Simmons flags targeting traps: skyscrapers, any building that says 'go through corporate' or points to a vendors list, and connected buildings run by a management company that may only run RFPs once a year. He tells operators to work individually managed standalone or medium-size buildings instead [ZDdd0TDbbFo @ 00:02:58]. On his own first bank walkthrough, AJ arrived 20 minutes early with a laser measure and learned the branch manager was not the decision-maker; a regional manager would judge the bid straight on the number by phone [IMsJ1NxKfUk @ 00:04:39]. OctoClean Media's closer calls 'are you the decision maker' a rookie question and instead asks how the last decision was made, by committee or by one person [1tf8JMWxi98 @ 00:03:25]. Map the buying chain on the first visit, or the proposal lands on a desk that cannot sign it.

After the signature, the traps shift to operations and labor. Steve Hansen of The Janitorial Store warns that small favors snowball: a client adds one extra here and another there until crews are doing 6 to 7 unbilled tasks and more than 30 minutes of free work. His fix is work orders, billed additional work, and starting that conversation at the prospect stage [EL4NN_-rX7o @ 00:09:27]. Matt of Commercial Cleaning CEO endorses free cleanings to build proof assets, meaning two to five written reviews, Google five-star reviews or video testimonials, but draws a hard line: 'Now, I wouldn't clean for free recurring forever' [SU1OB2thaKo @ 00:15:20]. On subcontracted labor, Matt's caller Dalen vets cleaners on their own supplies, insurance, and a test clean at an aunt's house, where the aunt asks about rebooking directly to see whether the cleaner poaches the client [o6xwPfuhTI4 @ 00:05:50]. Matt also tells operators to reject net 30 and net 60 terms and pay within 5 to 7 days of being paid, so subcontractors stay loyal instead of drifting [o6xwPfuhTI4 @ 00:18:59]. Slow pay and an unbilled scope both erode the margin you fought for at the proposal stage, and neither shows up until the first month closes.

callout.title: Four Checks Before the First Contract Goes Live
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, a reversal, or a hard warning a named practitioner reported. Clear all four before you sign, staff, or expand.
items: Run the bid through production rates and a margin floor before it leaves your hands; Adams targets 30 percent and only goes to about 25 percent for strategic accounts [ONLY MAIDS PODCAST — aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:08:41].
Write alarm, locks, lights and calling-security procedures into the proposal, because silence on security cost a $50,000-a-year account [Cleaning Launch — V84a_KWRYU4 @ 00:07:28].
Set the work-order and additional-billing rule during the prospect conversation, not after extras have already piled up [The Janitorial Store — EL4NN_-rX7o @ 00:11:09].
Expand to the next account only when current accounts are running smoothly [ONLY MAIDS PODCAST — aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:23:04].

action_checklist: Build a list of 50 qualified prospects from Google Maps, logging name, address, phone, website, contact and date, and go after the office, property, facility or operations manager rather than the receptionist [Janitorial Empire — 8ireVJkHvoo @ 00:01:48].

Run the six-question pain funnel in order: tell me more, how long has this been a problem, what have you tried, did it work, has it cost you time or money, have you given up [OctoClean Media — 1tf8JMWxi98 @ 00:01:40].

Arrive 20 minutes early with written questions and a laser measure, and use the lobby wait to scan for cobwebs, ledge dust, floor smudges and window fingerprints [AJ SIMMONS — IMsJ1NxKfUk @ 00:02:41].
Send the proposal within 24 hours of the walkthrough [ONLY MAIDS PODCAST — aQj7G__L-iE @ 00:09:17].
Follow up the same or next day, again a few days later referencing the walkthrough, then directly by end of week [OctoClean Media — OzSRs5osKKI @ 00:07:05].

At onboarding, set expectations for week 1, 30 days, 90 days and year 1, then cover emergency contacts, entry, alarms, QC, breakage, damage and additional work [The Janitorial Store — EL4NN_-rX7o @ 00:00:52].

chapters.question_prompt: Which outreach channels reliably generate commercial cleaning leads, and how do practitioners run them?
chapters.title: Prospecting Engine: Cold Calls, Cold Email, Doors, and Paid Search
chapters.subtitle: Cold-call scripts and live calls, appointment-setter training, reaching property managers, cold email campaigns, door-to-door sales, CTA targeting, free and low-cost lead methods, the 21-ways list, SEO and Google Ads case studies
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners selling commercial cleaning contracts agree the first touch opens a door rather than closes a deal: the ask is a walkthrough or permission to follow up, never a price over the phone, and the money arrives across 5 to 8 touches. Volume is the baseline, with owners at 20-50 dials a day against trained setters at 240-400, and Carolyn Arellano's funnel turning 100 calls into 1-2 walkthroughs. Street mechanics include Lemlist plus D7 Lead Finder email sequences, Prosp.ai LinkedIn cadences, saved Google Maps door routes, and Google Ads that Clicks Geek ran at $95 per conversion and a 24% conversion rate. Disagreements center on who should dial, whether to ask for a meet-and-greet or a walkthrough, and whether property managers can be reached cold, with The Profitable Cleaner's property-manager guest pointing to trade groups like IFMA.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the cold-calling camp, the first call is treated as a door-opener, not a closing event. Carolyn Arellano frames it bluntly: “Think of cold calling as opening a door, not closing a deal,” and she reports it takes 6–8 touchpoints, logged in a CRM or spreadsheet and paired with email sequences [xJ6TUBTc4Qo @ 00:01:58]. Matt at Commercial Cleaning CEO builds his whole CTA Targeting framework on the same idea: what you want from the key decision maker is “permission to follow up,” then you follow up roughly monthly or every other month aimed at the appointment, and he warns that pestering with weekly asks or manipulating your way into a quote hurts your reputation [turpTn9YjJA @ 00:04:35]. The Profitable Cleaner backs it with the numbers he cites: 80% of deals close after the 5th follow-up and 60% of salespeople never make a 3rd, adding “Follow-up still closes deals” [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:45:56]. Daniel Linton tells his appointment setters, “I cannot stress to you guys how important it is to be setting follow-ups,” and names high call volume plus follow-up management as the most important thing in the job [B415KkGunUw @ 00:05:39]. The operator takeaway is consistent: the money sits in the second through sixth touch, so the system has to remember the prospect even when the rep does not, and the cadence has to stay polite enough that the buyer keeps picking up.

The second agreed rule: the ask on the phone or at the door is a walkthrough or a meeting, never a price. Anton Pantio names asking for quotes instead of walk-throughs as the second big mistake owners make, and says his live booking landed because the setter offered a free walkthrough in a relaxed tone at mid-morning, where a 4:30pm dial would have gone to voicemail [-1k_o5iWj8w @ 00:00:36]. Daniel Linton drills two lines into his setters, “We never want to pitch the gatekeeper” and “We never want to offer a better price over the phone,” because pricing depends on the site, such as tile versus carpet, and has to be seen in person [B415KkGunUw @ 00:09:56]. AJ Simmons runs the same logic door to door: “your goal is to go in there and get a decision maker,” then move through point of contact, appointment, proposal and close, carrying a laser measure in case a walkthrough happens on the spot [VNrAGY4xXig @ 00:01:48]. Matt at Commercial Cleaning CEO adds the gatekeeper posture: “seem warm local and get them to like you,” because pushing for a quote with the wrong person is “way too soon” [turpTn9YjJA @ 00:03:52]. The common prerequisite is a process where every touch has one narrow objective, and that objective is the next conversation with the actual buyer.

Third, nobody claims one channel carries a company. The Profitable Cleaner says “there's no silver bullet,” runs cold call, cold email, LinkedIn and door-to-door together, adjusts by market because New Jersey differs from Texas, and calls COVID-era wins “fool's gold,” noting that mass emails to 500 property managers no longer work [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:05:18]. Volume is the other shared baseline. Carolyn Arellano's funnel needs 50–100 calls a day, ideally 100–200, because 100 dials yield only 20–30 reached, 10–15 conversations, 3–5 qualified and 1–2 walkthroughs [xJ6TUBTc4Qo @ 00:03:26]. Anton Pantio says most owners make 20–50 calls a day while his agents make 250–400, and his line is “You don't need a hundred perfect calls, you need one clean process repeated a hundred times” [-1k_o5iWj8w @ 00:07:51]. Rick Brown at Cleaning Launch stacks scraped lists, an offshore Philippines calling team at 2,000–5,000 contacts a week, cold email, 50–200 walk-ins a week, referrals and a Google Business Profile he says brings one or two contracts a month, and reports a walkthrough close rate of about 30% with a sales process versus 10–15% without [vAsWtmVSISA @ 00:01:23]. The baseline: a target list, a daily quota in the hundreds, and at least two channels running in parallel.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the phone, the scripts converge on a short qualify-and-book sequence. Jeremy Dixon opens with “can I speak to the person in charge of your janitorial services,” asks if they are open to a quote, then qualifies on current provider versus in-house, facility size and services needed before taking an email and scheduling the visit; one live call booked an overnight-cleaning prospect for “Tuesday at 1” [-LFfJivPXKw @ 00:02:41]. Daniel Linton's booking rules are tighter: ballpark square footage only, confirm the address rather than ask for it, push back once for name and email, confirm the decision maker, check whether corporate allows an outside vendor, then book 2–3 days out, Monday to Friday, 9 to 5 [B415KkGunUw @ 00:13:54]. His floor for reps is 30 dials an hour, 240 per shift, about 50% answered and calls averaging 3:30 or less, with the best reps booking about 6 meetings a day and week-one reps targeting 2 [B415KkGunUw @ 00:30:43]. The Profitable Cleaner opens with “help me out” and goes silent, closes with a two-option time choice, qualifies on frequency, square footage (10,000 sq ft, about 6,000 cleanable) and areas to improve, then sends a calendar invite and calls to confirm on the day [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:15:39]. Every version ends the same way: an email captured, a time locked, and a confirmation touch before the visit.

Cold email is run as a short sequenced campaign with a reason-to-switch hook. The Profitable Cleaner uses Lemlist at about $65 a month: a 3-email sequence with 1-day and 2-day waits (he has run up to 5), responders pulled automatically, sends every 6 minutes between 7:30am and 6:30pm, fed by D7 Lead Finder at about $30 a month and a list cleaned in ChatGPT to dedupe and strip info@ addresses, aiming for roughly 60% perfect data [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:27:10]. Constantin Schröck's property-manager campaign pulled 8 positive replies between November 12 and December 3 [Q5K2zTuisJc @ 00:00:00]. Email 1, subject “{Location} Management,” claims 2–3x faster work from proprietary equipment and asks to drop in and quote for 2025; email 2 is a case study (a week for the old vendor, two days for them, at lower cost); email 3 asks for a referral to the right person; email 4 is a breakup [Q5K2zTuisJc @ 00:04:22]. On LinkedIn, The Profitable Cleaner's Prosp.ai sequence (view profile, like a post, connect with a note, AI-written observation, voice note, then a “busy or just not interested” breakup) sent 135 requests in one week for 24 accepts and 23 conversations, with total software around $100 a month [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:37:07].

For inbound, the numbers come from the paid and organic specialists. Clicks Geek reports a janitorial Google Ads account on a $100 daily budget producing 2,200 impressions, 94 clicks, a 4.1% CTR, a $23 CPC, $2,100 spend and 23 conversions at $95 each, a 24% conversion rate against a 20–25% target, with keywords built as janitorial or commercial cleaning plus city or zip, and budget raised $25 a week while cost per conversion holds [EuwGlvViI4w @ 00:01:28]. Matt at Commercial Cleaning CEO justifies the spend with lifetime value: a $1,000-a-month contract is $12,000 a year and $60,000 over 5 years; he turns off automated bidding, caps the budget, sets max CPC from Keyword Planner, reports $100–$300 per conversion, and says “Don't go don't give Google the power to go spend your money” [esIqvQsbxco @ 00:12:04]. SEO Growth Partners took NextGen Cleaning from launch to 8–10 qualified commercial form leads a month plus 4–5 qualified calls within 1.5 years using real city pages with local photos, service landing pages and a fully built Google Business Profile linked from the site footer [1A40YzhpJ5Q @ 00:01:43]. On doors, The Profitable Cleaner builds a saved Google Maps list and spends 3 hours once a week hitting 25–35 businesses on a roughly 90-minute route [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:44:33].

callout.title: Small Moves That Get You Past the Front Desk
callout.body: Four field-tested adjustments the operators use to raise connect and booking rates without adding headcount.
items: Open with a neighbor link such as “we just started serving that facility next door” before your name or company name, because buildings take hundreds of calls a day [Commercial Cleaning CEO — f9f6YA_kX78 @ 00:00:55].

Read the phone number before you dial: an 844 or 1-800 number means a call tree, while a local 303-style number signals a privately owned business worth calling direct [The Profitable Cleaner — u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:12:01].
When a prospect asks where you are based, give their own city; Linton's setters do this across about 90 served cities [Daniel Linton — B415KkGunUw @ 00:09:39].
In a December send, ask to quote for the coming year; Schröck used “quote for 2025” because December is a slow month for property managers [Constantin Schröck — Q5K2zTuisJc @ 00:04:22].

sop_steps.title: Build and clean the target list
sop_steps.action: Google-map-hunt image-driven buildings, pull contacts, and clean the list before any outreach.
sop_steps.detail: Check the building and the leadership page for the GM or controller, pull emails with D7 Lead Finder at about $30 a month, then dedupe and strip info@ addresses in ChatGPT until roughly 60% of the data is clean [The Profitable Cleaner — u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:31:07].

sop_steps.title: Run the daily dial block
sop_steps.action: Dial in the high-answer windows at volume and log every touch.
sop_steps.detail: Call Tuesday to Thursday between 9–11am and 1:30–4:30pm, aim for 50–100 calls a day and ideally 100–200, ask about current provider, frequency and renewal date, and track 6–8 touchpoints in a CRM or spreadsheet [Carolyn Arellano — xJ6TUBTc4Qo @ 00:04:46].

sop_steps.title: Qualify and book the walkthrough
sop_steps.action: Confirm decision maker and vendor rules, then lock a meeting inside business hours.
sop_steps.detail: Get ballpark size, confirm the address, push back once for name and email, confirm the decision maker and whether corporate allows an outside vendor, then book 2–3 days out, Monday to Friday, 9 to 5 [Daniel Linton — B415KkGunUw @ 00:20:17].

sop_steps.title: Confirm the meeting and drip the rest
sop_steps.action: Send a calendar invite, call to confirm on the day, and keep non-bookers on a slow drip.
sop_steps.detail: Qualify on frequency, square footage and areas to improve, send the calendar invite, call to confirm the day of the meeting, and drip on everyone else every 90 days or so [The Profitable Cleaner — u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:23:30].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether the phone or the handshake should carry the pipeline. Carolyn Arellano argues calling beats door-to-door outright: two to three hours of dialing covers more ground than a full week of visits, and the Arellano funnel runs 100 calls to 20-30 reached, 10-15 conversations, 3-5 qualified and 1-2 walkthroughs [xJ6TUBTc4Qo @ 00:00:59]. AJ Simmons runs the opposite playbook on foot, working 10 doors an hour, carrying a laser measure in case a walkthrough happens on the spot, and telling reps to accept that 100 doors buys one customer [VNrAGY4xXig @ 00:13:05]. Commercial Cleaning CEO lands in between, treating door knocking as a two-visit play where reps don't rely on the front desk, return the next day, and nine times out of ten the contact agrees to receive information before the walkthrough offer lands [esIqvQsbxco @ 00:18:59]. The Profitable Cleaner's property-manager guest rejects the cold-volume camp for that buyer: the guest says property managers cannot be reached by cold call, email, or cookies, and points vendors to trade organizations, word of mouth, educational seminars, IFMA, and CAI for vetted, insured firms [phVhAxusau8 @ 00:00:18]. Channel choice follows the buyer, and property managers are the one segment where cold volume gets flagged as dead weight.

The second fight is over what to ask for on the first live connect. Anton Pantio names asking for quotes instead of walkthroughs as a core owner mistake and trains callers to book only a free walkthrough, delivered in a relaxed tone at mid-morning [-1k_o5iWj8w @ 00:00:36]. Daniel Linton's appointment-setting floor still leads with a free, no-obligation quote, but forbids offering a better price over the phone and holds pricing for the site visit because tile versus carpet changes the number [B415KkGunUw @ 00:09:56]. Commercial Cleaning CEO argues both asks are often premature: in the CTA Targeting framework the gatekeeper phase targets a conversation with the key decision maker, the decision-maker phase targets only permission to follow up, and the quote comes after an appointment that secures an agreement to cooperate, which the channel says makes price not a make-or-break factor [turpTn9YjJA @ 00:04:35]. The Profitable Cleaner compares a meet-and-greet against a direct walkthrough ask and prefers the meet-and-greet, opening with 'help me out,' staying silent, and closing on a two-option time choice [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:13:24]. Volume shops push the walkthrough hard; relationship shops trade speed for a softer first ask.

Paid search splits the field just as sharply. Commercial Cleaning CEO opens the free-methods playbook by warning owners against simply spending $100 to $5,000 a month on ads, and points companies under $10K a month toward past employers, family, friends, church and club networks, current clients, past bids, and neighbor discounts first [wC3VDZWQwZk @ 00:01:08]. The same channel still runs Google Ads, but with no automated bidding, a capped budget, and a max CPC pulled from Keyword Planner, justified by a $1,000-a-month contract being worth $12,000 a year and $60,000 over five years [esIqvQsbxco @ 00:12:04]. Clicks Geek reads a $100-a-day account with a 24 percent conversion rate as a client who is simply limited by budget and should raise spend to get more leads [EuwGlvViI4w @ 00:02:15]. SEO Growth Partners bypasses ad spend entirely, reporting that NextGen Cleaning reached 8 to 10 qualified commercial form leads a month plus 4 to 5 qualified calls within 1.5 years of launch, driven by real city pages, a fully built Google Business Profile, and service landing pages [1A40YzhpJ5Q @ 00:00:01]. The operator call is sequencing: free relationship channels when cash is thin, capped manual paid search once a contract's lifetime value can carry a cost per lead.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common phone failure is opening wrong. Commercial Cleaning CEO says buildings get hundreds of calls per day, so leading with your name, your company name, or what the company does gets filtered instantly; the fix is a personal link such as a nearby account or a similar facility, followed by one novel benefit [f9f6YA_kX78 @ 00:00:28]. The same channel flags a second self-inflicted wound at the end of the call: asking 'when should I reach out' hands control to the prospect, where the stronger move is asking permission to stay in touch and then feeding monthly-to-quarterly value [f9f6YA_kX78 @ 00:04:38]. Daniel Linton's setters lose bookings by pitching the gatekeeper; the rule is never pitch the gatekeeper, repeat the person's name back, get the decision maker's name and in-office time, and schedule a callback [B415KkGunUw @ 00:06:42]. Anton Pantio adds a timing trap from a live booking: the same relaxed, mid-morning call that landed Mona, a 25,000 square foot facility cleaned seven days a week, would have hit voicemail at 4:30pm [-1k_o5iWj8w @ 00:03:20]. Each of these losses lands in the opener or the final ask, before pricing ever comes up.

Cold email has its own graveyard. Commercial Cleaning CEO reports up to $500,000 in quotes from mass email in one month, but warns that pushing 1,000 sends a day out of a Gmail account risks blacklisting the sender [esIqvQsbxco @ 00:15:55]. The Profitable Cleaner calls COVID-era wins fool's gold and says blasting 500 property managers no longer works; the replacement stack is Lemlist at about $65 a month running a three-email sequence with one-day and two-day waits, sending every six minutes from 7:30am to 6:30pm and auto-removing responders [u3njpVGKi3M @ 00:04:41]. Constantin Schröck's fix for the incumbent-vendor wall is to hand over a concrete reason to switch, because most property management companies already have a vendor; Email 1 claimed 2 to 3 times faster work through proprietary equipment, and the third email, a referral ask for the right person's name and email, produced most of the eight positive replies [Q5K2zTuisJc @ 00:03:06]. On the inbound side, SEO Growth Partners warns that copy-pasting one city page 17 times or generating 50 pages overnight with ChatGPT or Claude is not legitimate, and built real city pages with local photos instead [1A40YzhpJ5Q @ 00:01:43]. Volume without differentiation is the shared failure.

The economics checks are blunt. Clicks Geek's March 2020 janitorial account spent $2,100 on 94 clicks from 2,200 impressions at a $23 cost per click for 23 conversions, a $95 cost per conversion against a $60 to $70 target, and the scaling rule is raising the daily budget $25 a week only while cost per conversion and conversion rate hold steady [EuwGlvViI4w @ 00:03:10]. Commercial Cleaning CEO puts paid-search cost per conversion at $100 to $300 and tells owners not to give Google the power to spend their money, which means no automated bidding, manual max CPCs from Keyword Planner, and a capped budget [esIqvQsbxco @ 00:12:04]. Anton Pantio warns that bought appointments often show up to a prospect who has no idea who you are, so Pantio's setters pass the lead and the cleaning company calls back to schedule [-1k_o5iWj8w @ 00:05:11]. Cleaning Launch shows the margin hit on the subcontract route: the prime keeps 30 to 40 percent, with a $3,000 contract paying the sub $2,300 to $2,500 [vAsWtmVSISA @ 00:06:54]. Before scaling any channel, run a contract's lifetime value, which Commercial Cleaning CEO frames as $60,000 over five years on a $1,000 monthly account, against cost per lead, setter fees, and any prime's cut.

chapters.question_prompt: What bidding methods and formulas do professionals use to price commercial cleaning accounts profitably?
chapters.title: Bidding Methods: Production Rates, Square Footage, and Hourly Formulas
chapters.subtitle: Production and billable rates, per-square-foot versus per-hour bidding, going sq-ft rates, bid formulas, three ways to price for win and profit, density and beginner pricing mistakes, and ISSA bid-like-a-pro sessions
chapters.executive_summary: Commercial cleaning bidders from OctoClean, Clean Biz Network, The Janitorial Store, CleanGuru, 7 Figure Cleaning, and Clean Ops Guide agree that recurring janitorial work is priced on labor hours, not a flat cents-per-foot number: measure cleanable square footage yourself, divide by a production rate you have tested on your own crews, then multiply hours by visits, 52 weeks, divided by 12, and a loaded billable rate. Rates in play run from 3,000 to 5,000 square feet per cleaner-hour, bill rates of roughly 1.2x to 2x the going janitor wage, a 40/30/30 labor-expense-profit split, and 3 to 5 percent for supplies. The divide comes on square footage: AJ Simmons and CleanGuru reserve per-foot pricing for floor and specialty work, while Darian Jarrett and Rudy Perez run a 19-to-20-cent-per-foot check alongside the hourly bid and split the difference.

key_metrics.label: Hourly bill rate multiplier
key_metrics.value: Double the cleaner wage ($15 paid becomes $30 billed); up to 2.5x still guarantees profit
key_metrics.context: AJ Simmons sets the customer hourly rate by multiplying whatever is paid to the cleaner by two, so profit is built into every bid without per-foot guesswork.

key_metrics.label: Per-account cost split target
key_metrics.value: 40% labor / 30% other expenses / 30% profit
key_metrics.context: Rudy Perez aims every account at 40 percent labor, 30 percent for supplies, insurance, taxes, and CPA, and 30 percent profit, using a $40 hourly charge in the worked example.

key_metrics.label: Monthly supply charge
key_metrics.value: 3% of base monthly rate ($64.98 on a $2,166.66 base)
key_metrics.context: Carolyn Arellano adds 3 percent of the base rate as the average monthly supply cost and bills it on top of the labor figure.

key_metrics.label: Cleanable square feet per occupant
key_metrics.value: About 200 cleanable sq ft per employee (20 employees is about 4,000 sq ft)
key_metrics.context: Matt Stowe uses headcount to estimate cleanable space on the qualifying call when the prospect does not know it, to decide whether the job clears the minimum bid.

sections.title: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Nearly every operator teaching bids lands on the same conclusion: you are selling hours, and square footage is only the input that gets you to hours. AJ Simmons of the Clean Biz Network compares two identical 5,000-square-foot buildings, one all hard floor with glass and tons of cubicles that eats four hours, one light office with three occupants that gets knocked out in an hour to an hour and a half, and concludes you cannot bid commercial cleaning by the foot [7VHAkhs_HG4 @ 00:03:35]. Dan at CleanGuru says that across more than 20 years building a sizable company, the number that mattered was how long a building should take per visit, multiplied by an hourly billing rate [UdGEmUdlNJs @ 00:02:42]. Clean Ops Guide runs the same test on two 10,000-square-foot buildings, a carpeted professional office with two restrooms versus a medical office with 12 exam rooms, and lands on double the labor for the second [9ojOIxznBUc @ 00:02:16]. Square footage gives context, Clean Ops says; the scope tells you the work, and labor determines the cost. Matt Stowe of OctoClean names density as the blind spot beginners keep hitting: bidding an open car showroom like a cube farm, then losing money on trash cans and desks nobody counted [45JohGIULbI @ 00:00:54].

The second point of agreement is that a production rate, meaning square feet one cleaner covers in an hour or minutes per fixture, is the prerequisite to bidding anything, and that borrowed rates are a crutch. Matt Stowe tells new owners to learn the business before bidding regularly, because knowing how long it takes you to clean a toilet, a sink, a floor, or a carpet matters more than any bidding app [SXNq_81x8SY @ 00:00:52]. At ISSA 2024, Matt called the ISSA cleaning times a lowest-common-denominator figure for average employees and said a trained crew should test, test, and test until it beats them [zAGjNnpTUcY @ 00:12:07]. Steve Hansen of The Janitorial Store is blunter: the heck with industry averages, because running somebody else's numbers means you never reach the true profit number on a job, and bidding software may just use those averages to calculate your time [baQYWkWt7lQ @ 00:01:28]. The shared warning underneath is that the owner's own pace is not a production rate until hired staff can repeat it. Matt says companies in this industry fail miserably once the core owners walk away from the job and the employees they hire cannot reproduce the work [SXNq_81x8SY @ 00:01:30].

Third, the walkthrough is a measuring job. Matt tells salespeople not to trust the square footage the prospect hands over, to measure every single thing, and points out how often a rep comes back with a great bid only for operations to find four restrooms nobody accounted for [zAGjNnpTUcY @ 00:20:54]. AJ's method is a laser measure pointed wall to wall, length times width for every area, summed into cleanable square footage rather than the whole building [vqE3IAR7B18 @ 00:05:55]. Once the hours exist, the speakers agree the hourly figure cannot be the cleaner's wage alone: Matt's follow-up breakdown says bidding is production rates, labor costs, material costs, back-office expenses, and other overhead, plus your profit [cVCpNgEj_zc @ 00:01:04]. There is also wide agreement on where per-foot pricing does belong. Carolyn Arellano quotes routine janitorial and commercial cleaning by the hour but prices carpet, tile, and VCT stripping and waxing by the square foot, the same split AJ uses for strip-and-wax, carpet cleaning, and pressure washing [IJlyq2UAXqU @ 00:01:14]. The prerequisite list that falls out is short: a tested production rate, a measured building, a tight service schedule that spells out what the crew will and will not touch, and a loaded rate before a number goes on paper.

sections.title: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The arithmetic is the same chain everywhere: cleanable square feet divided by production rate equals hours per visit; hours times visits per week times 52, divided by 12, times a billing rate equals the monthly recurring charge. Steve Hansen's production-rate method shows it with real numbers: a 12,500-square-foot account that takes 3.25 hours works out to 3,846.15 square feet per hour, cleaned three days a week that is 42.25 hours a month, and at a $22 billing rate the invoice is $929 plus any city or state sales tax [rGpgBfBHKg0 @ 00:00:58]. Steve also bends the rate for frequency: 3,500 square feet an hour on a five-night office drops to about 3,000 at three nights, because more soil builds up between visits [baQYWkWt7lQ @ 00:04:07]. Rudy Perez of 7 Figure Cleaning uses 3,000 to 5,000 square feet per cleaner-hour, picks 4,000 on a 50,000-square-foot building for 12.5 hours a night, bills $40 an hour for a $500 daily rate, and multiplies by 22 cleaning days instead of four weeks to land $11,000 a month [1_z-Kgj0GYM @ 00:01:35]. Clean Ops Guide rounds up deliberately, turning a 4,500-an-hour office into 2.5 labor hours and a 2,000-an-hour medical office into 5 [9ojOIxznBUc @ 00:04:17].

The billable rate is where the numbers get specific. Matt Stowe defines the cleaner minimum wage as the going rate incoming janitors actually earn in your territory, not the state, city, or county minimum, then multiplies it by 1.2 to 1.5 and has gone as high as 1.75 in California; $18 times 1.5 gives a $27 bill rate [zAGjNnpTUcY @ 00:23:04]. In OctoClean's formula breakdown Matt says companies typically run 30 to 35 percent for overhead plus profit, and builds high, medium, and low prices at 50, 35, and maybe 25 percent markup [SXNq_81x8SY @ 00:06:06]. AJ Simmons itemizes instead: pull the after-hours cleaner wage from Indeed or Monster, say $15, add about $3 for payroll tax and roughly 50 cents an hour for supplies to reach $18.50, then stack a flat $12 for profit to bill $30.50, which lands close to double the wage, the shortcut AJ leans on [vqE3IAR7B18 @ 00:09:26]. Steve Hansen has seen commercial billable rates from $18 to $55 an hour, holds one general-cleaning rate regardless of building size or frequency, raises it only for floor care such as strip-and-wax or marble polishing, and tells owners to survey competitors and sit in the middle of the local span [baQYWkWt7lQ @ 00:06:50].

Three worked examples show how the math closes. Carolyn Arellano's formula adds headcount: hourly rate times hours per visit times employees times days per week times 52, divided by 12. At $25 an hour, 4 hours, 5 days, that is a $2,166.66 base, plus 3 percent, or $64.98, for monthly supplies, and the client sees one monthly figure and the visit count, never the man-hours [IJlyq2UAXqU @ 00:06:46]. Matt's fixture method anchors on the restroom person: ISSA puts a toilet, sink, or urinal at about three minutes, OctoClean rounds to four, so 10 fixtures is 40 minutes, rounded up to 0.75 hours, times three team roles, times five days, times 52, divided by 12, roughly 49 labor hours a month, with the manager told the job takes no more than 48 [zAGjNnpTUcY @ 00:25:26]. AJ reverse-checks margin: a one-day-a-week, two-hour job pencils to $264 a month, gets rounded up to an in-house minimum of $275, and instead of a 70/30 subcontractor split handing over $192.50, AJ pays about $160, roughly $18 an hour for two hours at 4.33 visits a month, keeping $115, a 42 percent margin, because on accounts that small AJ wants 40 to 50 percent [vqE3IAR7B18 @ 00:15:43].
